summary:
Chocó is a department of Colombia on the Pacific coast, standing under the national framework of Colombia. No Chocó-specific legal provision, enforcement practice, or documented incident against a trans person was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment carried by the parent record applies.

What bears on Chocó is the territorial violence and displacement inflicted by armed actors. Reporting on Colombia's armed groups frames being queer in parts of the country as signing one's own death sentence, and killings continued at the hands of armed gangs even after the viral Millerey video shocked the country. In neighbouring departments armed groups have run 'social cleansing' campaigns, distributing flyers naming trans people as legitimate military targets and forcing trans women to flee at night under threat; eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023. Trans women are displaced from departments such as Chocó, where armed groups rather than departmental police regulate conduct.

Protection as victims of armed conflict is the element of the national framework relevant to Chocó: a national LGBTI policy text covers rights in public education, health care, prisons, and as victims of armed conflict, and national entities may not refuse to recognise same-sex couples. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, the right to change legal gender has been recognised since 1993, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage was legalised in April 2016, and same-sex couples gained joint adoption rights in 2015.
tangentialFactors: The Caquetá 'social cleansing' campaign documented in July 2024 is a separate department, but it illustrates the pattern of armed-group targeting of trans women that displacement from Chocó forms part of. Discrimination limits trans women in affected departments mainly to hairdressing or sex work, narrowing economic options for those who remain or arrive.

A national LGBTI policy text sets rights in public education, health care, prisons, and as victims of armed conflict, and national entities may not refuse to recognise same-sex couples.

In practice, armed groups rather than departmental police regulate conduct in the department, and trans women have been displaced from Chocó. Protection as victims of armed conflict is the element of the national framework with direct local bearing.
outOfScopeNotes: No Chocó-specific incident, arrest, enforcement action, or departmental ordinance against a trans person was located in the inventory; the region-specific signal rests on displacement reporting and the armed-group pattern observed in neighbouring departments. Whether Chocó's own police or courts have applied the national facilities judgments or the trans-detainee rulings is not sourced here.
